why_how.text: Turning on your headlights during rain or reduced visibility is required by law and increases your visibility to others.
Wet pavement is most dangerous at the start of a light rain, when oil, dirt and water form a slippery film that weakens road contact on curves and lengthens stopping distance, so reduce your speed.

On wet pavement tires wipe the road like a windshield wiper at speeds up to thirty-five miles per hour, a standard passenger vehicle begins to hydroplane partially at about thirty-five miles per hour, and at fifty-five miles per hour the tires ride entirely on the water film, leaving no friction to brake, accelerate or corner.
In a severe rainstorm tires lose all contact with the road at fifty-five miles per hour, and a gust of wind, a curve or a slight turn can then create an uncontrollable skid.

To reduce hydroplaning slow down in rainstorms, on slushy roads and in standing water, keep tires properly inflated and replace them when the tread wear indicators show, because deep treads let water escape and can prevent complete hydroplaning at normal highway speeds.

Never drive across a flooded roadway, because as little as six inches of water can float some smaller vehicles and two feet of water will carry most vehicles away, after which the vehicle may roll and fill with water, trapping everyone inside.

Motorists trapped in their vehicles account for nearly half of all flash flood deaths in the United States, victims often drive straight off the edge of an eroded road without knowing it is gone, and flooding is especially hard to recognize at night.
If your vehicle stalls on a flooded roadway leave it immediately and seek higher ground, because it is better to be wet than dead.
Partial hydroplaning begins at about thirty-five miles per hour, while at fifty-five miles per hour the tires ride entirely on the water and lose all contact in a severe rainstorm.

why_how.text: Defensive driving means being prepared through the practice of good driving habits, which are as easy to form as bad ones and should begin the moment you step into the vehicle and be used on every trip, short or long.
Bad driving habits come from laziness, impatience, inattention, arrogance and aggressiveness, and a driver who shows any of them must evaluate and adjust that behavior to drive safely.

A lazy driver looks only in the rear view mirror instead of turning the head to look behind before changing lanes, pulling away from the curb or getting out on the traffic side, and failing to signal before turning, changing lanes or leaving the curb is a related bad habit that can cause a serious crash.

Regardless of traffic you must come to a complete stop at a stop sign or red light even when turning right, and an impatient driver who speeds from stop to stop, weaves through traffic and tailgates disrupts traffic and raises the chance of a crash without realizing it.

A good driver sits up straight with a firm grip on the wheel, knows where the vehicle is and watches developing traffic problems, because a driver who leans back, loosens the grip and lets attention wander lets the vehicle wander too, and driving with an arm out the window, chatting, gesturing or ignoring the traffic flow marks an inattentive driver.

While the impatient driver is simply in a hurry, the arrogant or aggressive driver is purposely in a hurry, treats the vehicle as an extension of the ego, shows little respect for traffic laws or the rights of others, and should neither be imitated nor competed with.

Concentration is one of the most important elements of safe driving, so the driver's seat is no place for daydreaming, mental napping, window shopping, scenic viewing or distracting conversation, because driving an automobile is a full-time job.

Pressure from vehicles behind and an empty cross street tempt the impatient driver merely to slow for a stop sign, yet a complete stop is required at every stop sign or red light even for a right turn.
